name: Sta. Rita Hills
summary: A cool AVA in western Santa Barbara County, where hills running east to west let Pacific fog and wind reach the vines. About two thirds of the vineyard is Pinot Noir, followed by Chardonnay.
label_note: Under federal rules, at least 85% of the wine must come from grapes grown in the AVA named on the label, and the wine must be finished in the state, or one of the states, where the AVA lies.

name: Santa Maria Valley
summary: A funnel shaped valley opening west to the Pacific, where morning fog and afternoon wind keep it cool and the growing season long. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay lead, with some Syrah, and the grapes keep plenty of acidity.
label_note: Under federal rules, at least 85% of the wine must come from grapes grown in the AVA named on the label, and the wine must be finished in the state, or one of the states, where the AVA lies.

name: Russian River Valley
summary: A cool Sonoma County valley that begins about 10 miles from the Pacific, where morning fog and a wide swing between day and night keep acidity in the grapes. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir make up over 70% of the harvest.
label_note: Under federal rules, at least 85% of the wine must come from grapes grown in the AVA named on the label, and the wine must be finished in the state, or one of the states, where the AVA lies.

name: Columbia Valley
summary: Washington's largest AVA, a dry basin in the rain shadow of the Cascades that holds over 99% of the state's vineyards. Warm days and cool nights on loess over flood deposits give ripe fruit while keeping natural acidity.
label_note: Under federal rules, at least 85% of the wine must come from grapes grown in the AVA named on the label, and the wine must be finished in the state, or one of the states, where the AVA lies.

name: Walla Walla Valley
summary: A valley shared by Washington and Oregon at the foot of the Blue Mountains, cooler and wetter than much of Washington, with loess over flood deposits and basalt cobbles in the south. Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Merlot lead.
label_note: Under federal rules, at least 85% of the wine must come from grapes grown in the AVA named on the label, and the wine must be finished in the state, or one of the states, where the AVA lies.

grapes.name: Syrah
grapes.local_note: Close to half the vineyard in The Rocks District.

appellations.name: The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater
appellations.note: Sub-AVA in Oregon, on basalt cobblestones, first set out in a 2015 rule (27 CFR 9.249).

name: Santa Cruz Mountains
summary: A cool mountain AVA between the Pacific and San Francisco Bay, the first in California defined by its mountain topography, much of it above the fog line. Plantings are split about evenly among Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay.
label_note: Under federal rules, at least 85% of the wine must come from grapes grown in the AVA named on the label, and the wine must be finished in the state, or one of the states, where the AVA lies.

appellations.name: Ben Lomond Mountain
appellations.note: Sub-AVA, first set out in a 1987 rule (27 CFR 9.118).

name: Long Island
summary: An AVA covering Nassau and Suffolk counties, where the Atlantic, Long Island Sound and Peconic Bay temper the climate over sandy glacial soils. Merlot is the most planted grape, and the wines tend to be restrained and crisp.
label_note: Under federal rules, at least 85% of the wine must come from grapes grown in the AVA named on the label, and the wine must be finished in New York.

name: Niagara Peninsula
summary: Canada's largest viticultural area, on the south shore of Lake Ontario and crossed by the Niagara Escarpment, whose slopes and lake breezes shape the climate. Riesling, Chardonnay and Cabernet Franc lead, and Icewine is mostly made from Vidal.
label_note: A VQA wine naming Niagara Peninsula needs at least 85% of its grapes from there, all from Ontario, and vinifera grapes only, except Vidal for Icewine. Icewine grapes must freeze on the vine and be picked at minus 8°C or colder.

name: Okanagan Valley
summary: British Columbia's largest wine region, running over 250 km from the US border to Armstrong along Okanagan Lake. Summers are hot and dry with cool nights; the cooler north suits aromatic whites and the hot south bold reds.
label_note: A BC VQA wine may name Okanagan Valley when at least 85% of its grapes come from it and the rest from elsewhere in British Columbia.
